turns.prompt_text: This print came out nearly perfect but is a little warped at the very end Because of that warp, it doesn't sit correctly aligned I wonder if I could sand the end? And then try and level and print on top of it Probably not, but I wonder what other practical solution there is Attached 2 files. - d621b887-b0d6-46d1-b142-359c6e975856 - 006d288c-509b-4fff-843a-cd73e739d678
turns.response_html:
The short answer is no, you can't easily level it and print directly on top of it.

Once a print warps off the build plate, the geometry shifts in Z, meaning the nozzle would either smash into the raised warped edge or print into thin air over the lower sections. Pausing, homing, and perfectly aligning a warped part to resume printing is a recipe for a nozzle clog or a ruined toolhead.

However, you have a few practical recovery options depending on how much material needs to be removed and what the part is used for.

Option 1: Sanding & Post-Processing (The Quick Fix)

If the warp is minor and the part doesn't require absolute, injection-molded precision to function, manual correction is the easiest route.

  • Sanding: Secure a piece of coarse sandpaper (80 to 120 grit) flat on a workbench or piece of glass. Rub the warped face of the print against it in a figure-eight motion to ensure even pressure. Keep checking the squareness with a flat surface until it sits level.
  • Heat Re-shaping: If it's printed in PLA, it has a low glass transition temperature (~$60^\circ\text{C}$). You can dip the warped end into hot water (just below boiling) or gently use a hair dryer to soften the plastic, then press it firmly against a completely flat surface to straighten it out while it cools.

Option 2: The "Split and Glue" Method

If you need the full height of the part but don't want to re-print the entire object, you can slice the model in your slicer to save time and filament.

  1. Measure the Warp: Determine exactly where the warping begins to distort the geometry.
  2. Cut in Slicer: Use the Plane Cut tool in Bambu Studio to slice off the warped section from the digital model.
  3. Print the Patch: Print only the section that was ruined by the warp.
  4. Join Them: Sand the flat mating surfaces of both the original print (after cutting/sanding away the warped bottom) and the new patch, then bond them together using Cyanoacrylate (Super Glue) or 2-part epoxy.

Preventing It Next Time

Since the rest of the print looks incredibly clean with crisp layer lines, your settings are mostly dialed in. To prevent that specific edge from lifting on the next run:

  • Add a Brim: A 5–8 mm outer brim acts like an anchor for sharp corners or curved edges prone to peeling.
  • Clean the Plate: Give your build plate a thorough scrub with warm water and dawn dish soap. Finger oils are the number one killer of first-layer adhesion.
  • Check for Drafts: Ensure there are no AC vents or open windows blowing cool air toward the printer, causing uneven thermal shrinkage.

Are you hoping to preserve the exact total height of this specific piece, or is it just the flat mating alignment that matters most for how it functions?

turns.prompt_text: I think option two of slicing it would be a practical fix because then I could adhesive it on
turns.response_html:
The "split and glue" method is definitely the most practical way to salvage the hours and filament you’ve already put into the main body. It saves you from starting over from scratch while guaranteeing a perfectly flat bottom surface.

Since you are using a Bambu Lab printer, you can use the built-in cut tool directly in Bambu Studio to make this seamless:

How to execute the split:

  1. Measure the cut height: Use a pair of calipers or a ruler to measure exactly how many millimeters up from the base the warp extends until the print becomes perfectly straight.
  2. Use the Cut Tool: Import your model into Bambu Studio, select it, and click the Cut tool icon on the top toolbar.
  3. Position the Plane: Set the Z-height of the cutting plane to match the measurement you took. Keep the orientation horizontal.
  4. Discard the Bottom: Make sure the slicing mode is set to keep the top part, and you can discard or uncheck the bottom section.
  5. Print the new base: Flip the remaining model piece so the newly cut flat surface is face down on the build plate, add a 5mm outer brim to guarantee this patch doesn't warp too, and print it.

Tips for a rock-solid bond:

  • Scuff the joint: Lightly sand both mating surfaces with some 120–220 grit sandpaper. Giving the plastic a little bit of "tooth" makes a massive difference in how well the adhesive grips.
  • Adhesive choice: Regular Cyanoacrylate (Super Glue) works incredibly well for a quick bond, but if this part is going to experience mechanical stress or impacts, a 2-part epoxy will give you a much stronger, structural joint.
  • Alignment: Because this part has a distinct curved profile, use the outer walls as your alignment guide while pressing the pieces together. You can wrap a tight piece of painter's tape around the seam while it cures to keep it from shifting.

Give the cut a shot in the slicer—it's a great workflow trick to have in your back pocket for large prints!
